summary: Defines a way to prevent and detect BGP route leaks by using roles in OPEN and UPDATE messages. Route leaks violate assumed relationships between networks, such as sending a route from one provider to another. Previous approaches depended on operator configuration without checking it matched. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Each network tells its neighbor what role it plays, so mistaken advice that breaks the rules can be caught.

questions: how to prevent bgp route leaks

subtitle: Neighbors agree on their business roles when a BGP session opens, and routes are tagged so leaks can be stopped and spotted.

tldr.problem: Route leaks happen when a BGP route is passed along in a way that breaks the expected relationship between networks, for example from one provider to another. Existing prevention depends on operator configuration with no check that both sides agree.
tldr.mechanism: Each eBGP speaker advertises a BGP Role in the OPEN message, and the two sides must declare matching roles. Routes are then marked with an Only to Customer (OTC) attribute that stops them travelling in the wrong direction.
tldr.outcome: Leaks can be prevented at the local AS and detected several hops away. The mechanism covers IPv4 and IPv6 unicast and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9234 is a Proposed Standard, published in May 2022. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Route Leak Problem
sections.content:
A route leak is the propagation of BGP prefixes that violates assumptions about how networks relate to each other. Examples are announcing a route learned from one transit provider to another transit provider or to a lateral (non-transit) peer, or announcing a route learned from a lateral peer to another lateral peer or to a transit provider. The RFC says these are usually the result of misconfigured or absent route filtering, or of poor coordination between autonomous systems.

Existing approaches mark routes by operator configuration, with no check that the configuration matches what the eBGP neighbor has, and no enforcement that the two speakers agree on the relationship. This RFC replaces that with an in-band method: a new configuration parameter, the BGP Role, negotiated in the OPEN message, plus an optional transitive path attribute called Only to Customer (OTC). The focus is the Internet, meaning IPv4 and IPv6 unicast route advertisements.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a network passes on a message it was never supposed to pass on, like a student forwarding a private note to the whole class. This RFC adds a way to catch that.

sections.title: Peering Relationships and Roles
sections.content:
The relationship terms here describe restrictions on route propagation, sometimes called the Gao-Rexford model, and do not have to match payment agreements. Provider, Customer and Peer are synonyms for transit provider, customer and lateral peer in RFC 7908. The roles and their rules are:

  • Provider: MAY propagate any available route to a Customer.
  • Customer: MAY propagate routes learned from a Customer, or locally originated, to a Provider. All others MUST NOT be propagated.
  • Route Server (RS): MAY propagate any available route to a Route Server Client (RS-Client).
  • RS-Client: same limits as a Customer, toward an RS.
  • Peer: MAY propagate routes learned from a Customer, or locally originated, to a Peer. All others MUST NOT be propagated.

A relationship built from these roles is a normal peering relationship. If the local AS has more than one role with the same remote AS (for instance Provider-to-Customer for some prefixes and Peer-to-Peer for others), the relationship is called Complex.
sections.eli5: A provider is like a big shop selling to you, a customer is you, and a peer is a friend at your level. Each kind of relationship has rules about what you may tell whom.

sections.title: The BGP Role Capability
sections.content:
One role SHOULD be configured on each eBGP session, based on the local AS's knowledge of its own role, except when the connection is Complex. Roles are confirmed through the BGP Role Capability in the OPEN message: code 9, length 1 octet, with a value for the speaker's role. If a role is locally configured, the speaker MUST advertise the capability, and MUST NOT advertise multiple versions of it.

When both sides send the capability, the roles MUST correspond: Provider with Customer, RS with RS-Client, and Peer with Peer. If they do not, the speaker MUST reject the connection with the Role Mismatch Notification (code 2, subcode 11). Multiple identical capabilities are treated as one; multiple differing ones are rejected the same way.

For backward compatibility, if a role is sent but none is received, the speaker SHOULD ignore the absence and proceed, using its locally configured role. An operator may choose a strict mode in which the remote capability is required, and a missing one causes rejection with the same notification.
sections.eli5: Before talking, both sides say their role. If one says provider, the other must say customer. If the stories do not fit, the call is hung up.

sections.title: The Only to Customer Attribute
sections.content:
The OTC attribute is an optional transitive path attribute of the UPDATE message with type code 35 and a length of 4 octets. Its value is an AS number. Its purpose is to enforce that once a route is sent to a Customer, a Peer or an RS-Client, it afterwards goes only to Customers.

On receipt (ingress):

  1. A route with OTC received from a Customer or RS-Client is a leak and MUST be considered ineligible.
  2. A route with OTC received from a Peer whose value is not the Peer's AS number is a leak and MUST be considered ineligible.
  3. A route received from a Provider, Peer or RS without OTC MUST get OTC added, set to the remote AS number.

On advertisement (egress):

  1. A route going to a Customer, Peer or RS-Client without OTC MUST get OTC added with the local AS number.
  2. A route that already has OTC MUST NOT be propagated to Providers, Peers or RSes.

Because the attribute is set at the local egress or, if the remote AS does not support this specification, at the local ingress, the value is the same either way. That makes the scheme more robust and benefits early adopters. Once set, OTC MUST be preserved unchanged.
sections.eli5: Think of a stamp that says 'downhill only'. Once a letter has it, it can only be passed down to customers, never back up or sideways.

sections.title: Edge Cases and Error Handling
sections.content:
An OTC attribute whose length is not 4 is malformed, and the UPDATE is handled with “treat-as-withdraw” from RFC 7606. That RFC documents possible negative impacts such as forwarding loops or dropped traffic.

Roles MUST NOT be configured on a Complex session. If a Complex relationship can be split into separate eBGP sessions with normal relationships, roles SHOULD be used on each of them. The RFC also says the mechanism is NOT RECOMMENDED between ASes inside an AS Confederation; if OTC is added on egress from a confederation, it MUST carry the confederation identifier. Private AS numbers behind an Internet-facing ASN are allowed, but on egress OTC MUST NOT carry anything other than the Internet-facing ASN.

The procedures apply only to AFI 1 (IPv4) and AFI 2 (IPv6) with SAFI 1 (unicast), MUST NOT be applied to other address families by default, and the operator MUST NOT be able to modify them. The document does not specify special handling of an incorrect AS number in OTC.
sections.eli5: A broken stamp means the letter is thrown out. A few odd setups, like a club with many members acting as one, get special rules.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of BGP in RFC 4271 and RFC 4272 apply. A misconfigured role can change how far prefixes spread: a downstream link set to Provider or Peer limits what can be advertised toward customers, while an upstream provider wrongly set as Customer may propagate routes learned from other providers or peers. Role negotiation and confirmation make such mistakes unlikely.

Making strict mode the default could stop an eBGP session coming up after a software update, so such defaults are strongly discouraged. Removing or changing OTC can reduce leak detection, and an on-path attacker could remove it and leak the route to a transit provider. The RFC notes this kind of threat is not new in BGP and that BGPsec (RFC 8205) protects only the AS_PATH attribute. Adding OTC on a Customer-to-Provider advertisement, for example for traffic engineering, is discouraged because it limits propagation unpredictably.
sections.eli5: Someone could scrape the stamp off a letter to fool others, or a wrong role could stop mail going where it should. Careful setup avoids both.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the BGP Role capability as value 9 in the Capability Codes registry and created a “BGP Role Value” subregistry. Values: 0 Provider, 1 RS, 2 RS-Client, 3 Customer, 4 Peer. Values 5 to 255 are assigned by IETF Review.

IANA also registered the OPEN Message Error subcode “Role Mismatch” as value 11, marked the values 8 to 10 as Deprecated because of improper use, and registered the “Only to Customer (OTC)” path attribute with code 35.
sections.eli5: The official number list was updated so everyone uses the same numbers for the new role label and the new stamp.

items.label: Provider
items.desc: The local AS is a transit provider of the remote AS.

items.label: RS
items.desc: The local AS is a Route Server.

items.label: RS-Client
items.desc: The local AS is a client of a Route Server.

items.label: Customer
items.desc: The local AS is a transit customer of the remote AS.
